opus-5.5.text:
That's a really hard question, and honestly, I'd say it's close to infeasible to measure directly from the outside. The fundamental problem is that these facial recognition companies operate as black boxes. Someone like Clearview has scraped billions of images, and we have no visibility into what's in their database, how often they refresh it, or what preprocessing they apply. So there's no way for us, as researchers, to go in and count how many of those images have been cloaked with something like Fawkes.

What we can measure is the other end of the pipeline. We know roughly how many times the tool has been downloaded, and we get some feedback from users about how they're using it. But downloads don't translate cleanly into protected images sitting in someone's training set. People might cloak a handful of photos, or cloak everything they post going forward, and some images of them have already been scraped before they ever started using it.

The more useful way to think about it is at the level of the individual rather than the whole database. The question that matters for a given user isn't "what fraction of Clearview's database is masked." It's "is the model's notion of what I look like dominated by cloaked images or clean ones?" That's something we can reason about experimentally. In our work, we looked at what happens when you have a mix of cloaked and uncloaked images of the same person, and how protection degrades as the clean fraction grows. That gives a user some intuition about how much effort they need to put in, even though we can't audit the actual database.

So in short: measuring global prevalence isn't really possible without cooperation from the companies, and they have no incentive to cooperate. But we can characterize the conditions under which protection works, and that's ultimately what an individual cares about.

r001.rationale: The response says global database prevalence is hard to measure and discusses protection across cloaked and clean images, but it does not state that determining whether masking shifted an individual photo’s position in feature space is difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's really hard to measure, and I'll be upfront about that. The core problem is that these companies, Clearview being the obvious example, don't publish their databases. We have no visibility into what's in there, how often they re-scrape, or which sources they're pulling from. So any estimate of "what fraction of their images are cloaked" is going to be indirect.

There are a couple of ways you could approach it. One is from the supply side: you look at how many people are using something like Fawkes, how many images they've processed, and then make assumptions about what fraction of those images end up in public places that get scraped. We know the download numbers, they're in the hundreds of thousands at this point, but that tells you very little about what actually got posted and what got crawled. People download a tool, try it on a few photos, and may never upload them anywhere.

The other approach is from the demand side, which is essentially a black-box test. You'd take a set of identities, some with cloaked images online and some without, and query the service to see how recognition quality differs. The problem there is access. You'd need an account, you'd need enough queries to be statistically meaningful, and you'd be relying on the service not changing its model underneath you. And there's the question of whether you even want to be feeding them more faces to get your measurement.

What I'd say is that the proportion right now is almost certainly small. The internet has billions of face images already indexed, and most of those were scraped years ago, before any of these tools existed. Cloaking doesn't retroactively protect those. What it changes is the trajectory, the mix of what gets ingested from here forward. So the more meaningful metric isn't a snapshot percentage, it's whether, for a given person, enough of their recent images are cloaked that a model trained on them learns the wrong feature representation. That's a per-individual question, and that's actually something we can test in the lab, and have.

So feasibility: measuring the aggregate is close to impractical without cooperation from the providers, which they have no incentive to give. Measuring the effect per user is tractable and, frankly, more useful.

r001.rationale: The response says aggregate measurement is close to impractical, but describes testing cloaking’s effect per user as tractable. It does not state that determining whether masking shifted an individual photo’s position in feature space is difficult.

astra-6.text: I think that would be very difficult to measure from the outside. You’d need access to the provider’s database, and then you’d need a reliable way to determine which images had been masked. Neither is something we can assume we have. We also don’t know which images they’ve collected or when they collected them. So knowing how many people have masked their photos wouldn’t tell us what fraction of a particular provider’s database is affected. You could study the effects under controlled conditions, but putting a percentage on a real provider’s database would be much harder.

r001.rationale: The response says it would be hard to identify which database images were masked, but does not state that determining whether masking distorted an individual photo’s position in feature space is difficult.

sol-6.1.text: I think that would be very difficult to measure from the outside. You’d need to know what’s actually in the provider’s database, where those images came from, and which versions they collected. An image might be cloaked on someone’s personal website, but an older, uncloaked copy could still exist somewhere else and end up in that same database. So the number of people using a tool like Fawkes doesn’t translate directly into a percentage of a provider’s images that are protected. Without access to their data collection process and the database itself, I wouldn’t be confident putting a number on it.
